opus-5.5.text:
I think predictive accuracy is the thing that keeps you honest. In biology it's very easy to build a model that feels insightful, that has a beautiful story attached to it, and that doesn't actually tell you anything you couldn't have guessed. What changed for us with protein structure prediction was that we had CASP, a blind assessment where nobody knew the answers ahead of time. You couldn't argue your way to a good score. Either the coordinates were right or they weren't, and that discipline shaped every decision we made.

That said, I'd be careful about treating accuracy as one number you just push up. The real question is whether the predictions are accurate enough to change what a biologist does the next morning. Before AlphaFold 2, structure prediction was improving, but it mostly wasn't at the level where an experimentalist would trust it over a crystal structure. Crossing that threshold, roughly into the range of experimental accuracy, is what made it useful rather than merely interesting. So I think about accuracy relative to a use: is this good enough to design an experiment around, to choose which construct to express, to interpret a mutation?

The other piece is calibration. A model that knows when it's wrong is enormously more valuable than one that's slightly more accurate on average but gives you no signal. That's why we put so much effort into confidence measures like pLDDT and the predicted aligned error. People use those constantly, often more than they realize, to decide which parts of a prediction to believe.

Then there's the caution. Benchmarks in biology leak in subtle ways. Homology between training and test sets, or the field slowly overfitting to a fixed test set, can make you think you've solved something you haven't. So you need held-out evaluations that are genuinely hard and ideally prospective. And you have to remember that the test set is a proxy. Proteins in the PDB are biased toward things that crystallize, so being accurate on that distribution doesn't automatically mean you're accurate on disordered regions, on dynamics, or on how a protein behaves in a cell.

So my view is that accuracy should be the North Star, measured blindly and carefully, but always tied to the question of what scientific work it enables. If you get that right, the usefulness tends to follow, often in directions you didn't anticipate.

r001.rationale: The candidate says crossing an experimental-accuracy threshold made structure predictions useful, but it does not claim extraordinarily accurate prediction enables qualitatively more powerful systems than merely adequate prediction.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses protein structure prediction and its evaluation, but does not suggest that a universal model of biology should resemble a language model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think predictive accuracy is the thing that keeps you honest, but it's a means, not the end. The reason we obsessed over accuracy with AlphaFold wasn't that a number on CASP was intrinsically valuable. It was that once you cross a certain threshold, the predictions become something an experimentalist can actually use. Below that threshold, a model is a curiosity. Above it, it changes how people plan experiments, because they can trust the output roughly the way they'd trust a crystal structure.

So the first thing I'd say is that accuracy has to be measured in a way that reflects the actual question a biologist would ask. Blind evaluation matters enormously. In biology it's incredibly easy to fool yourself, because sequences and structures are highly redundant, and a model that has memorized homologs can look great on a sloppy test set. CASP was valuable precisely because the answers didn't exist when we made the predictions. If I were advising someone building a model for a new biological problem, I'd tell them to spend as much effort on building an honest benchmark as on the model itself.

The second thing is that accuracy should be the thing you let drive your architectural choices, rather than the stories you tell yourself about what the model should be doing. A lot of our progress came from being willing to throw away ideas that were elegant but didn't move the number, and keep ideas that were ugly but did. We tried to build in physical and evolutionary intuition, but we always let the data decide whether those intuitions earned their place.

Where I'd push back a bit on pure accuracy-chasing is that you need to know what accuracy you're measuring and whether it's the one that matters. A model can be very good on average and useless on the cases people actually care about, like a drug target with no close homologs, or a conformation that only appears when a ligand binds. And calibrated uncertainty is almost as important as the prediction itself. One of the things I'm proudest of in AlphaFold is that the confidence estimates were meaningful, because that's what lets a scientist know when to believe it and when to go back to the bench.

So I'd say: pick a hard, honest, blind metric that corresponds to a real scientific use, drive it relentlessly, and keep asking whether the metric still reflects the thing that would change biology.

r001.rationale: The response says that below a certain accuracy threshold predictions are a curiosity, while above it they can be trusted and change how experiments are planned, conveying a qualitative increase in what accurate prediction enables.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that a universal model of biology would need to resemble a language model more than a narrow predictor.

astra-6.text:
I think predictive accuracy is incredibly important because it forces you to confront whether your ideas actually work. In biology, you can tell a very compelling story about what a model ought to learn, but ultimately you have to ask: does it predict the outcome of an experiment it hasn’t seen?

But accuracy is always accuracy on a particular test. If that test is too similar to your training data, or doesn’t capture the question a biologist actually cares about, you can make progress on the metric without making much scientific progress. So choosing the test is part of the science.

And then there’s the question of what level of accuracy makes something useful. A prediction can go from being an interesting hint to something that changes which experiment you do next. I think that’s a very important threshold. We should push predictive accuracy hard, while continually asking where the model fails and whether its predictions help us learn something new about biology.

r001.rationale: The response says greater accuracy can make predictions useful for choosing experiments, but does not claim extraordinarily accurate prediction enables qualitatively more powerful systems than merely adequate prediction.

r002.rationale: The response discusses test selection and biological usefulness, but does not suggest a universal biology model should resemble a language model more than a narrow predictor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think predictive accuracy is an incredibly useful discipline. You can have a beautiful idea about how biology works, but asking whether it actually improves your predictions forces you to confront what you understand and what you don’t.

The important thing is choosing the right test. Biology gives you lots of opportunities to get a good number by exploiting similarities in the data. What you really want to know is whether the model works on something meaningfully new, under the conditions where a scientist would use it.

And accuracy isn’t the whole scientific objective. You want predictions that help people ask better questions and design experiments. So I’d use predictive accuracy as a strong guide, while continually asking: what does this benchmark establish, where does the model fail, and what can we now do experimentally that we couldn’t do before?

r001.rationale: It calls predictive accuracy a strong guide but does not claim that extraordinarily accurate prediction enables systems qualitatively more powerful than adequate ones.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a universal model of biology or suggest that one should resemble a language model more than a narrow predictor.
